utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we give an opportunity to the OTP to re-examine the witness, Mr. Emmerson --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I did understand there was a matter you would like to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There is. It's, in fact, two related matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: One involves a correction to a position I indicated on the transcript at the end of last Friday when Your Honour was asking questions about the locations of interviews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But the first which is related concerns the document which I hope that Your Honours have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have received a document, first page being the Department of Justice, Office of the Medical Examiner, death certificate. And then attached is a longer document, disaster victim identification, and -- which gives -- the first document seems to give a cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Gun-shot wound to the pelvis", and the second document, at least at the last page, bears the text: "The above-mentioned person was dressed with KLA uniform."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That's the one. Just to indicate what these documents are. First of all, collectively they are 65 ter number 934, and I would ask that they be marked for identification. The first document, as Your Honour indicates, is a summary post mortem report on Kemajl Gashi by Marek Gasior, an international forensic pathologist, which is dated the 17th of May, 2006. Thereafter, there is a lengthy document dated the 10th of August, 2005, which is, in effect, a missing persons report. And Your Honours will see that the reporting person is identified as Mustafa Gashi, that's on the first page, for the father's name and on the third page, which is for some reason numbered page 8 at the bottom, as the reporting individual, the name and telephone number of the father, Mustafa Gashi is there given. And Your Honours will see that, again, on the first substantive page, which is, as I say, curiously numbered 6 at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The place where the missing person was last seen is given as Barane and the date as July 1998. And as Your Honours picked up in the concluding pages, that's the page which is -- bears the number 19, the circumstances of disappearance, again, are repeated: "Went missing in a village of Barane." And then on page 21, in amplification of an otherwise silent description of clothing and appearance, the report records that the above-mentioned person was dressed with KLA uniform. Family, that is, other than the individual reporter, family doesn't know any details about the clothes. It is our understanding that this witness was present at the time when this information was provided. The second point to some extent relates to the first. That was the first substantive document disclosed by the Prosecution to the Defence in relation to this individual and this allegation in the indictment, and that notification came during May, there is the 19th of May service of DNA reports and the 31st of May service of this -- these documents. And on the strength of that and on the strength of the telephone number for the father there provided, Defence investigators visited the father in Pec to interview him about the content, and in particular the content of the last page of this report. It was during that meeting with the father that this witness first approached investigators for the Defence, so the first contact was made in Pec in the home of the father. What I need to correct is that Your Honour asked me at the end of Friday's proceedings where the interview was conducted and I said it was my understanding that the interview was conducted in Pec. In fact, after that first meeting, there was then a further meeting which that took place in Pristina with the witness attending the offices of the Defence investigation, and completing and signing the witness statement that Your Honour has seen. So it may be that some of the witness's answers appear to have some confusion in them, but perhaps the clarification is that this interchange took place in both locations, both in Pec and in Pristina. I hope that clarifies the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Emmerson, for that. There is one other matter which I would briefly like to address, that's the following: Protective measures have been sought in relation to Witness 6. The Chamber would like to receive as soon as possible a response to that, whether in oral form or in writing. Could you give us any indication -- Mr. Guy-Smith, I see -- could you give us any indication when the Chamber could expect a response?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe after consultation with my colleagues, we should probably be able to do that at the.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Then if --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Maybe after the next -- after the first break even.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You therefore intend to give the information orally I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We would then turn into private session at that moment. Then, Mr. Re, are you ready to -- for the re-examination of the witness? Then, Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, you asked the -- the 65 ter document 934 to be marked for identification. Are you going to put it to the witness or --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No. I'm going, if I may, in due course, depending on how Mr. Re deals with it, if he does, to tender it from the bar table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From the bar table. Mr. Re, would there be any problem in relation to that and is there any explanation for the document -- at least the first document starting on page 3 and then the second document starting on page 5 that suggests that there would be a page 1 and 2 somewhere as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The only explanation I could hazard would be that the first two pages are the cover pages from the organisation which sent it to the OTP. That's the normal situation with these things. That appears to be handwritten on the bottom, but I can certainly look into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would there be any problem as far as the Prosecution is concerned on admitting this document from the bar table?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Registrar, could you please assign a number to 65 ter 934.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit Number D96, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon, Mr. Gashi. The Chamber has decided that the counsel for the Prosecution will have additional time for re-examination. Mr. Gashi, it was a long weekend, but you'll certainly remember what happened last Friday. Last Friday you, during examination-in-chief and during cross-examination, you gave answers to questions which are -- were sometimes difficult to reconcile. I just mention KLA membership of your sister, when you saw your father for the last time, whether what kind of work he was doing when he was in Barane. I'd like to remind you that you gave at the beginning of your testimony a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. That means if a question is asked to you, if you don't know the answer, tell us; if you do know the answer, tell us as precisely as possible what the answer is. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Based on the discussions that this Chamber had with this witness last week and based upon what I now understand to be the potential areas of examination that Mr. Re may be entering -- and this may be an appropriate time for the witness to take off his headphones so that he's not privy to this conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you take off your earphones for a second. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In my last conversations, which were admittedly off the record with Mr. Re at the conclusion of the proceedings, hopefully Mr. Re is being attentive to what I'm about to say, there was a discussion about the extent and nature of examination that Mr. Re would engage in. It was my understanding Mr. Re was going to confine himself or believed it would be appropriate to confine himself to the facts and circumstances surrounding the taking of the Defence statement and no further than that. I'm not sure whether or not he still maintains that position. I, once again, raise the concerns that I raised last Friday with regard to the issue of counsel being given to this gentleman or him at least having the opportunity to have independent legal advice concerning the potential of criminal sanctions based upon the situation which we're in, independent of any inclination by any particular party. With regard to this witness, since the issue has arisen as a matter of law, I believe it would be appropriate for him to have independent advice of counsel so that he can make a determination of how best to proceed. And I would encourage -- I would encourage once again that that be afforded to this gentleman. I am not, obviously, in a position to pursue that; I have a different interest here. However, in order to deal with the, I think, relatively sensitive nature of the legal status that this particular witness has at this time I think it is something which is of great importance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber has considered whether or not to take any initiative to provide counsel to the witness. The Chamber has decided not to do so at this moment. At the same time, of course, the Chamber, if it comes to any question where -- where the witness could be expected to have a dilemma as to whether to incriminate himself, of course the Chamber will then raise the issue with the witness if it comes to any of these points. But at the moment, the Chamber will just wait and see. But if you would like me to specifically draw the attention, as I did last Friday, that not speaking the truth -- intentionally not speaking the truth once you've given a solemn declaration, that that is an offence with a maximum penalty under the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, then I'm willing to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe that it would probably be appropriate; however -- and I understand the Chamber's position with regard to at this point not offering the gentleman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- Independent counsel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- I do have a question because I -- quite frankly I'm of somewhat two minds here. One is the mind of an individual who is concerned about the protection of an individual, of a particular person's rights as a witness who may potentially be a defendant in some other proceedings which is really not my bailiwick here. And the other is obviously representing my client. I do not wish to be in a position where I continue to jump up like a jack-in-the-box with regard to my concerns about his potential rights. And don't wish to either be doing that or to offend the Chamber because determination made thus far with regard to how we should proceed. However, depending on the questions Mr. Re chooses to ask, and once again, I don't know whether or not he's going to limit himself as we discussed last Friday or he's going to go further then that, we could fast be approaching the very area that is of concern to the Chamber as of our last session and has been articulated by the Chamber with regard to the potential admonition that could be given at this time. I don't know whether it would be appropriate, for example, for the Chamber to consider at this point in time granting the witness immunity for his prior testimony or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In my submission, we're nowhere near that point at the moment. In our submission -- in the Prosecution's submission any differences in his testimony last week are reconcilable. I don't intend to suggest to the witness that he's not telling the truth in any way. I wish to explore certain matters with him. If it came close to the point where, in our submission, the Trial Chamber had to warn the witness, I would certainly stand up and proffer that advice, but in my submission we're not there yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You see no inconsistencies irreconcilable last Friday?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sometimes an impression is given that someone is saying something which is irreconcilable. I'll just remind you that Mr. Emmerson's question at transcript 4880, he asked the witness if everything he'd said was true and then read to the -- in relation to the statement. He said: "And what you said to those people the truth, Mr. Gashi, did you tell them the truth? "A. The truth as far as I could recollect." Then Mr. Emmerson read the witness a large slab. Mr. Emmerson didn't ask the witness at the end whether what he had said -- what Mr. Emmerson had read to him on the record was true. So where you have a situation where someone has read four or five minutes' worth of transcript, after having said, Is it all true, and what follows, there's a lot of room there for confusion. So in my submission, we're not at the point where it's a position of lying as opposed to another explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May I respond briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Firstly, I don't think, with respect, this is the time to argue what inferences should be drawn from the witness's answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And secondly Mr. Re is just simply incorrect because at the end of that passage, I did ask him specifically and in terms in respect to the passages that I had read to him and that he'd signed whether they represented his best recollection at the time that he was interviewed by Defence investigators of the truth of the position and he replied yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's not exactly what Mr. Re said. But let's not -- Mr. Re said whether this would still be his answer at this moment. Or whether his recollection has -- therefore at this moment is different from what he stated at the time. Let's -- let's not continue this debate. Let's first give an opportunity to Mr. Re to -- to continue or to start re-examination. Mr. Gashi, I earlier said that you're earlier bound to tell us the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. I already told you Friday that it is an offence if you would not do so, so therefore carefully think about your answers. Mr. Re, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gashi. Can you hear me clearly?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It might assist if you just turn slightly towards me when I'm asking you questions. Could you do that. And look towards the Court as well. All right. I just want to ask you about your reading and writing ability. I think in your statement you said you had -- to the Prosecution you said you had eight years of primary school; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How old were you when you left school?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. 17 or 18, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I think in your statement you said it was 15 years, you were 15 year old. Does that assist?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It could be. It could be 15. I apologise. I was confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you left school, what sort of work were you doing?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mechanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you receive training to be a mechanic; that is, go to a technical college or something like that?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked as a mechanic, and I followed a course for a mechanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you do written exams for it?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No written exams but practical, working.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your reading and writing like when you left school?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What does "yes" mean? Could you read and write well?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can read well, but as for writing, I can't write that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could you read and write as well as the other pupils at school when you left?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you left school, did other pupils stay on at school and go on to finish their school years and you left early?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the others followed and I just left it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know who the accused in this case are or what the accused -- what is meant by "the accused"?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know of any of the people who were charged with any of the offences, do you know what that means, in this court?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What do you know? Tell the Trial Chamber what you know about it.

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know their names?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of one of them, yes, I know his name; and the other two, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What's the one -- whose name do you know?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know Ramush by his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know why they're here, the three of them?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know what the defence is or what's meant by the defence?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Defence, yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What do you understand is meant by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When Mr. Emmerson said to you on Friday that people from the Defence came to speak to you, what did you think he meant?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: On Friday, Mr. Emmerson said that people from the Defence had come to speak to you and had taken a statement from you. What did you think he meant when he said to you people from the Defence had come?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what to say. I don't know how to explain it to you. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you understand when he said that to you? What did you understand he was talking about?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in fact, I didn't understand anything, and as far as that statement is concerned I have no answers. And the least I could say here is that I'm not here to accuse anyone. I'm here only to testify about the statement that I gave to Sultan in Pristina, who brought me the news that he found my father. As far as other statements are concerned, I will not respond to those statements. I only can respond to the question -- to the statement I gave to Sultan. This is all I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gashi, may I just intervene for one moment. It appears that you have to be interviewed twice: Once by the person you called Sultan, and we have a written statement taken approximately one month after that first statement you gave. If there's any question put to you, whether in relation to with the one statement or in relation to the second statement, you'll have to answer these questions to the best of your knowledge. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know what the Prosecution is, Mr. Gashi?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prosecution, no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know what the difference between the Defence and the Prosecution is?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little bit, not that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber what you understand, what that little bit is.

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to explain it in words.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, try.

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know really.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We've heard evidence of two statements: One to Sultan and the other one to some other people, okay?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The statement to the other people, when they came to see you, who did you think they were?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Ramush's Defence, and they said that they were the Defence of Ramush.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you think that meant?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It meant that they were there to defend him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Defend him against what?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I don't know, against what. I didn't talk that long to them about this subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many Defence people for Ramush came to see you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I missed the answer in English -- oh, two persons, I see it now on the screen. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were they men or women?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Men.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did they -- what are their names, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did they leave you their cards?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where did you go to tell them your story?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to my house. I didn't tell anyone my story.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did they come to make the statement which has your signature on it or that you signed?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came in a car, in my house. First we went and had a coffee together; then, I think it was on the next day when they collected me, we went to Pristina. I gave a statement. Then I returned home again, and then a week or a week and a half later, I'm not sure exactly how long, one of them came back. We had a coffee together. He read the statement to me. I don't know whether it was in English or Turkish or whatever. He asked me if I could sign that. I signed it, and that was it, basically. I had no further contacts with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did these men speak to you in Albanian or another language?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: One spoke in Albanian and the other in another language.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did they type into a computer when you spoke to them or did they take notes on a piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Handwritten.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When they came back, did they ask you to make any changes to the statement or did they come back with a piece of paper and read it to you?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They just came and read it back to me and said to me, "Can you sign it?" I said, "Yes, I can." And that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did they give you a copy of it?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you see -- ever see a copy of that statement in Albanian?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The first time I saw it was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And when you saw it here, you saw it on a computer screen in English. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So had you had any access to that statement between September last year and last Friday when parts of it were read to you?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "yes"? I'll put it another way --

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. When these two men came to speak to you, did they audiotape or videotape you making the statement to them?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And how long were they with you the second time when they came back and read it to you?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only one person came back the second time, not the two of them. Altogether, it was about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the one who came back, was he speaking to you in Albanian?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Albanian, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did he ask you whether you wanted to make any changes to the statement?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember. It all lasted for half an hour. We had a coffee together. He read it to me. I signed it. And that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why did you go with them to make this statement in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they came and collected me and I went with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Presumably you had a choice about whether you went. Why did you decide to go with them to make this statement?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were any members of your family -- I withdraw that. Did you discuss with any members of your family whether or not you should make this statement before you went and did it?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have no one left from my family except for my wife. I have no one else to talk to about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Have you got a grandfather?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but we don't live together.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is his name Mustafa?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you -- did he talk to you about your statement to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are there members of your family who are supporters of Ramush Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, we all support him, me included.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Have you spoken to any of those members of your family who support Ramush Haradinaj about your coming here to testify?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what have they said to you about coming here to testify?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They thought I was joking. They didn't believe me when I said that I was going to come here to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Has anyone ever put any pressure on you not to testify or suggested that you shouldn't testify?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Has anyone tried to influence in any way by saying things to you about what you should say when you came here?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't discuss with anyone there this thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know whether your grandfather, that is, Mustafa, made a report about your father, Kemajl Gashi, a missing persons report to the Department of Justice in -- or Interpol or UNMIK in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To what I know, he made a report to the Red Cross. It was a teacher of mine, I think he reported to her, and she came to our place. I don't know if he made any other report with any other organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you ever with your grandfather when he made a report to anyone about your father's death?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When on Friday Mr. Emmerson read to you a number of parts of the statement you made to Ramush Haradinaj's Defence in September last year, what did you think he was doing or asking you when he read those -- read those passages to you on Friday?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't pay attention to that statement. He just read it, and I was in a hurry myself. I just signed it and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about on Friday when Mr. Emmerson, seated to your left over there, read to you large parts of it, what did you think he was doing or asking you when he read it to you?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, what did you think you were answering when he was reading it to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I object to this question. I object to the line of questioning as well. The transcript is clear. If Mr. Re wants to take the witness to a particular question and answer, that is another matter. But the questions I put to the witness both before and after putting passages of his statement to him are clear for all to see. And to ask him what the witness thought I was asking whilst reading a passage is liable, particularly given some of the answers that the witness has given, to produce nothing but an unhelpful response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, it may be clear that the witness is better in concrete matters than in abstract matters. Perhaps you could keep that in mind. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Between pages 4882 and 4886 -- excuse me for one moment. Between those pages Mr. -- On Friday afternoon, Mr. Emmerson read to you parts of the statement, and at the end of reading three and a half pages of transcript, those parts of the statement to you, he said to you -- or it's actually 4885, if I've misled anyone, I apologise. He stopped reading at 4885 and then went to the signature. The last question he asked you was: "You've signed that page also, Mr. Gashi. Was it true that you left things out of the witness statement that you gave to the Prosecution, either deliberately or by mistake?" And you answered: "Unintentionally." Now, I'm going to ask you to try and remember what things you left out of the statement to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing the video the other day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we perhaps explore that a bit more in detail. Mr. Re, I think the witness is better to be served with concrete examples. In the one statement you signed, you were asked whether your sister Ganimete was a KLA soldier. You said she was not. In the other statement a similar question was put to you -- at least you stated that your sister - and let me -- let me quote you also exactly. You indicated that your sister was in the KLA as well, just as you were. Now, in the one you leave out that your sister was in the KLA; as a matter of fact, you say she was not. Now, in the other statement you say she was. Do you remember why you said in the one interview that she was not a KLA member and whether in the other you said she was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know in which statement I said that my sister was in the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But is it right or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not. My sister was not in the KLA. She was staying with a family in Buqan. She was not wearing any uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But not wearing a uniform does not automatically mean that you are not in the KLA because there were KLA members who did not wear uniforms. So the question is not whether she wore a uniform, but the question is whether she was in the KLA.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did she ever do any work for the KLA? Not being a member but nevertheless --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I don't know. I was not there with her. I was in another place, she was in another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in the statement you gave, the second statement you gave, you said that your father was interviewed and so were you and Ganimete. That is a line - and I ask you to focus on Ganimete being interviewed - that does not appear in the first statement. Is that something you left out in the first statement or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would first --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There are a number of statements here and I'm not sure that the witness is necessarily fixed in a concrete manner as to which statement is which, which is why I rise, since he's indicated he's given a number of statements now and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that the questions are clear enough and I --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I was confused by your questions, which is why I rose. There are at least three separate times at which he's given --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, the Bench considers the questions to be clear enough, even if they do not give the dates of the statements. Mr. Gashi --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The reason I asked the question is because you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The question is whether you are dealing with the issue of memory or dealing with the accuracy of what was said. And since this arose from the context of what he did not remember telling and failed to include in one of the statements, it is yet unclear on the state of the record that we have right now which statement we're referring to. And that's the reason that I rise, for purposes of clarity and for no other purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gashi, in the one statement at least it's written down on paper that when you were asked -- no. Let me -- whether you -- I already paid attention to the question whether your sister Ganimete was or was not a member of the KLA. Now, in the second of the two statements we talked about, it is written down with your signature on the bottom of that page, and let me read the following. "My father, Kemajl, also later joined the KLA also at Barane. Straight away, he came under suspicion of being in some way associated with the Serb MUP. This was almost certainly because of his association with Nexhat who was generally believed to be a Serbian collaborator. He was interviewed and so were I and Ganimete." Now, in the statement, this is the statement you gave in September last year, in the statement given one month earlier there is no specific mentioning of Ganimete being interviewed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only speak about myself. In that statement I did not mention anyone, not Nexhat either. I only mentioned one statement, the statement that I gave to Sultan. As to other statements that another person or my sister gave, I cannot respond to questions related to those statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you signed that statement, and that statement has been given to this Chamber. So if I read portions of that statement, as Mr. Emmerson did last Friday, when you said that that statement was given to the best of your recollection, I would like you to answer the question here as well; that is, when you said that your father, you, and Ganimete were interviewed, was she?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't. As for myself, I wasn't. As for my father and Ganimete, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you heard your father screaming in the room next door --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you at that time interviewed? Were questions being put to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't know how to explain it to you. It was only three or four minutes. There was no interview by anyone at that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: On Friday, Judge Orie asked you about those bits of the statement which Mr. Emmerson over there read to you when you were sitting there, and you said: "Most of what is there is true but some is not true." Do you remember that, when the Judge -- Judge asked you that and you answered that?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did things that were not true come to be put into that statement? How did the untrue things get into it?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember when you were asked to sign it whether -- do you remember noticing untrue things in the statement at the time you signed it?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it earlier, that I didn't pay too much attention to what was read to me. He just read it to me and I signed it. I don't understand English. I wasn't given a copy, and I don't know how to respond to questions about that statement when I was not given a copy of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, there is -- in a previous answer that was on my list of questions still to be put to the witness. You earlier said, "It was read to me. I don't know whether it was Turkish or English."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, did you refer to what was on paper or did you refer to the language in which the statement was read to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was referring to what was on paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And in what language was the statement read to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In your own language. Yes. Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It was apropos of that last issue, apropos of the questions that Mr. Re has just been putting, and apropos of question and answer at page 16, line 25 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just a second, please, I might as well get the right -- 16, 25, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "Did he ask you whether you wanted to make any changes to the statement?" "I don't know. I don't remember." If Mr. Re is pursuing this line, in fairness, he ought to ask the witness about page 7 of the statement, where just above the witness's signature the passage appears --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but don't read it at this moment, Mr. Emmerson, because the witness is of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour sees the passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have drawn the attention to that part of the statement. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, also if I might, once again for purposes of clarity, the answer that was given on line 24 -- I'm sorry, page 24, commencing at line 15, if we could identify the he that he is referring to so that we're very clear who he is talking about each and every time he is dealing with such an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's unclear to me, Mr. Guy-Smith. I think the testimony of the witness was that when he was interviewed there were two persons, and when the one came back -- that when someone came back that it was one person. So I -- unless you have any other way of understanding that this was -- but of course we could -- let me put one question in this relation, in this context. Mr. Gashi, you said the statement was read to you when -- and there was, if I understood you well, one person that came later to see you, read it to you, and that you then signed the statement. I'm now talking about the second statement, that is, the statement you gave not to Sultan but to the other gentleman, yes? Was the person that came back and read out the statement to you, was that one of the two persons that earlier came to see you and interviewed you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, just to make my position absolutely clear in relation to the point that I raised just a moment ago in relation to page 7, so that it's clear for the record, the passage at the top half of that page is in Albanian and translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And the witness has signed both versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But it's not the same, as you may have noticed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: As between the top and the bottom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In terms of the Albanian versus the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. For example, I don't know whether you see any 8 -- I take it that that's a reference to pages --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. So the page numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so it's not the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think that we can have the verbatim translation of that upper passage but it is plainly in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's quite clear -- of course that's clear to me and I -- I asked you not to read it. I take it that Mr. Re has observed what you said. Whether you should have asked that in a further possibility to examine the witness or whether you should have intervened is another matter, but at least, Mr. Re, you notice that Mr. Emmerson has drawn your attention to page 7 of the statement, especially the -- the certificates in there. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Judge Orie a little while ago when I asked you about page 20, line 1: "Was it true that you left things out of the witness statement that you gave to the Prosecution either deliberately or by mistake?" And you answered to Mr. Emmerson: "Unintentionally." You said you couldn't remember which bits you'd left out, and the Judge asked if I could explore it with you in a little more detail. I'm just going to hand you a copy of your statement in the Albanian translation and if you can read through it and tell the Court if you can remember anything you've left out of this statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are now --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm showing the witness the Albanian translation of his English statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- Of August 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I think it's the 4th of August, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So what I want you to do is just to read through the statement. Are you okay with reading it, first of all?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can read it, but I don't know. It's been a year and I don't know what has happened from that time on. It's been a year since I gave this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. All I want you to do, if you can read it, is just to go through it and if you can remember anything that isn't in the statement but should be there, just tell the Trial Chamber what it is. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a statement of 32 paragraphs, which the witness might not be able to read right away. The Chamber suggests the following: We'll have a break. We'll invite the witness to read the Albanian version of his earlier statement. During the break he'll have an opportunity to point at matters which he thinks he should have stated at that time and which he does not find in the statement. You will have another five to ten minutes to continue your examination. Then the Defence will have an opportunity to further examine the witness, if there's any need to do so. Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could you -- yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm obviously entirely in Your Honour's hands as to whether you think this exercise that Mr. Re proposes to embark upon is a useful one, but it is plain as it possibly can be that this witness has made inconsistent statements. And for a witness now to be asked to read one statement where he has already made a subsequent statement in which he has said in terms and signed in terms, to say that he had left things out of the first statement and has then included a large number of things in the second statement which were not included in the first statement, which he has first avowed and supported and then disavowed on oath, it's entirely a matter for Your Honours whether for the record it would be of assistance to have the man say there is or there isn't anything I should have said in this statement. But frankly in my submission, we've reached the position where this is something of a charade and an attempt to bolster a witness whose ability to provide reliable evidence is manifestly reached a point where this type of questioning can't assist. That would be my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I join --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You join. And Mr. Harvey, you join as well. From the fact that the Chamber grants limited time for this exercise, although the time then to be used as good as it can be and not to wait here and sit for 15 minutes in court, you may understand from this approach that although the Chamber allows, to some extent, this exercise that the question as to the usefulness of it has been considered by the Chamber. Mr. Gashi, what we would like you to do is to read the statement that was just given to you, that's a statement in your own language. Mr. Re, in view of the limited time available, are there specific portions that you would like the witness to read? Is there a certain place where you would like him to start to read?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The main portions would be from paragraph -- paragraph -- sorry, paragraph 15 through to paragraph 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We would like you to read the statement starting at paragraph 15, reading the remainder of your statement. If there's any time left, of course you could also read the first paragraphs, but you're instructed to start reading at 15. And then after the break you could tell us whether, now having re-read the statement, whether there's anything that comes into your mind of which you say, Well, this is what I should have added or I should have told at the time. That's what we'd like you to do. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll have a break and we'll resume at five minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gashi, did you have an opportunity to read --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the statement? Did you read it entirely or just the portion down from paragraph 15?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From paragraph 15 to paragraph 32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Is there anything that now spontaneously comes into your mind? Did you say, Well, I left out something that I considered I should have said at the time? Is there anything of the kind that you would like to draw our attention to, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Then, Mr. Re, I think I said five to ten minutes. Should we make it eight?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't think I need eight, but I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You just said there's nothing you wish to draw our attention to. Is there anything you can remember leaving out that's not there that should be there?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember the video which we briefly showed you in court the other day. Just tell us, do you remember whether your father was in that video?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You couldn't see very well from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you could see your father in that video? Was he there? Did you see him?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could you see the Mete's office where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, you're putting two questions to the witness. He answers no. I did understand that you did not see your father on the video. Even if you don't see him on the video, was he there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In that video could you see the building or the office where Mete office was that you went to when you heard your father screaming?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Re. Mr. Emmerson, you are the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I wonder if Your Honour would just permit me one very short passage of further questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I wonder if we might have D92 up on the screen on page 7, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just focus in - yes, thank you very much - on the Albanian and a little lower down if we can just take it -- just to there. That's fine. Further cross-examination by Mr. Emmerson:

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gashi, can you see the screen clearly?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And can you see your signature there as the first of the two signatures on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Gashi, look at the bottom portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Go to the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You identified this as your signature in your evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one here, on the left --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you agree that that is your signature?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the other signature's signed by the gentleman who read the statement to you, isn't it, in your presence?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just go a little further up then please back to the signature we were looking at again.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The first signature there that's showing on the screen now, you signed that, Mr. Gashi, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So it is your signature; you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why did you tell us just a moment ago that it wasn't?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I thought it wasn't but then I saw the dot at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Perhaps we can just look at the Albanian again, please, go to the top of the page. Thank you. Pausing there for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you - unless the Trial Chamber would wish it - to read the Albanian out for the record. We can do that separately. Could you please read to yourself, just for yourself, the second of the two paragraphs that appear there, please. Just make sure you've understood it. Do you understand that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Does that paragraph say that you fully understand the statement that you have made and that it is true to the best of your knowledge and recollection? Is that what that paragraph says?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And that the statement is given voluntarily; correct?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now read the next paragraph, that's the third one down, to yourself, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It may be of assistance to the Trial Chamber if the witness were to read it aloud. It may clarify something.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm very happy for that to be done in which case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In which case perhaps you could start with the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could you, please, Mr. Gashi, start again at the top of that text, please, and slowly read aloud for us the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I have read this statement APO. This statement contains eight pages and it was read to me in Albanian."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now could you please read the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I fully understand this statement, and this statement is accurate to the best of my knowledge and recollection. I gave this statement voluntarily."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now could you read the third paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I was told that I can improve, change, or add anything that I wish to this statement."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And then the final paragraph there, please.

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I am aware that it may be used in the juridical procedures before the ICTY, that in the cases against the people who are responsible for various violations of the international law in the territory of ex-Yugoslavia from 1991 and that I will -- may be invited to testify."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And finally, please, the line that appears opposite your signature, what does that say? Could you read that for us, please.

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The signature of the person who gave the statement."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You have just been sent outside from the Tribunal for 20 minutes or so to read your own Prosecution witness statement, and in that time I think you told us you managed to read from paragraph 15 to 32. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You have no difficulty in reading the text in Albanian that's right in front of you now, do you?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I see. And you've signed there, Mr. Gashi. Can we assume that you read the Albanian there before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. Further cross-examination by Mr. Guy-Smith:

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Gashi, when you spoke with Mr. Sultan, did he audiotape or videotape you making the statement to him?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you see any tape recorder when you were being interviewed by Mr. Sultan when you made the statement to him?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you see any camera that was being used during the period of time that you were making the statement to Mr. Sultan?

utterances.speaker: MEDIN GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gashi, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you for coming to The Hague and for answering all the questions put to you by the parties and by the Bench. Madam Usher, would you please escort Mr. Gashi out of the courtroom, but not until I have wished you a safe trip home again, Mr. Gashi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, any exhibits left with this witness? We have not yet finally assigned a number to the -- to the documents we received today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to deal with the exhibits. I've still got on my list P325, which is a photograph; and P326, which is a series of photographs, school building. Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not -- then P325 and 326 are admitted into evidence. Then we have, numbering not being sequential, but D91, the statement of the sister of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D92 is the September 2006 statement by the witness given to the investigator of the Defence; and D96 being the two documents, Department of Justice, medical examiner, and disaster victim identification, in relation to the father of the witness. Any objections against the exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Certainly not against D92, nor the missing persons report to the Department of Justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D96. D91 then remains --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: D91 is the statement of the sister. It's -- she's not here to -- she's not a witness here. A passage of her statement was read to the witness. Normally, it should just remain at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say you have -- if the whole of the statement would be in evidence, there would have been no possibility for the Prosecution to cross-examine the witness. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The position is that this witness gave evidence that his sister had told him that she saw her father alive two weeks after he was last seen at the barracks, and both parties, and indeed the Trial Chamber, have explored with him the basis for the conclusion that what his sister said to him was capable of being dated as an incident that took place or a meeting that took place after rather than before the occasion when he saw his father, or rather, heard his father's -- the sound of his father screaming inside the barracks. In addition, he has given evidence to the Defence about having seen his father washing dishes in the kitchen and his sister, in her witness statement, says that he told her that at that time. Now, in our submission, this is an item of real evidence which is available for the Trial Chamber to consider. I recognise that the weight to be attached to those passages in the witness statement is less than it would be if she were here to give evidence and be cross-examined on them. But the hearsay he has already given about what she told him is in evidence, and therefore to have from the source of the hearsay statement the basis for her account in a statement given to the Prosecution, in our submission, if this count is persisted with, is material that should properly be before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, would you like to add anything to what you said earlier? Finally, it's objection or no objection. I mean, the Chamber will decide if the objection is there; if there's no objection, then finally the Chamber will not necessarily admit it but it's more likely that the Chamber will admit it. Does the objection stand or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: At the moment it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the moment it does, okay, then the Chamber will determine the matter. Then are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's also the witness's own statement the 4th of August, 2006. Now, it wasn't put on the exhibit list as such in the same way as D92 was but he did read the Albanian version of it and the Trial Chamber has seen it. But in my submission -- or I move for its admission into evidence although --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From the bar table.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And on the same basis as the sister's statement I have no objection to the Trial Chamber in this particular instance, having that statement admitted in evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then it should be assigned an exhibit number. That -- but have it -- do we have the -- we are now talking about the Albanian version of the August 2006 statement, which is not yet in evidence or we need it -- do you have a 92 ter number for it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We don't. Mr. Smith can have it in e-court in half an hour if it can be given a virtual number, shall we say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, have we already in anticipation of --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think we have it in the system, I'll give you the Defence document identification for it in just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We should have the Albanian because he read the Albanian. Both should go in, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Certainly the Prosecution statement in English which is the signed version and I think the original, unless I'm wrong, is Defence document identification 1D410001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This document, if admitted into evidence, should be in the two languages, the witness having read one of them and we were able to read the English version. Madam Registrar, that would be -- it -- although it comes from the Defence, it -- it's tendered by the Prosecution. That would be P ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this would be Exhibit Number P327, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence in the absence of any objection. Are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, the next witness is Mr. Jakup Krasniqi, will be taken by my colleague Mr. Kearney with Mr. Gosnell's assistance. And if Your Honours would excuse me and Ms. Schweiger.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the next witness is called may I respond to Your Honour's inquiry in relation to protective measures for Witness 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was informed, as a matter of fact, informally, and that should now be put on the record that there are no objections against the protective measures sought in relation top Witness 6. That's one. Second, there was a request from the Defence whether written submissions could be made in respect of -- in response to the written submissions made by the Prosecution in view of the Zyrapi exhibits. And that request is granted, although the Chamber does not expect very lengthy submissions there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, do I understand that the Prosecution is seeking admission under Rule 92 ter of the 23rd and 24th of May, 2007 statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, as well as also the transcript of the testimony of this witness from the Limaj trial in 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There may be some confusion there, because the statement gives a lot of annexes, of which it's unclear -- are you seeking the annexes to be admitted as well? Because you're also separately -- annex 12 was also part of your 92 ter motion and therefore some confusion is there. But perhaps we first start with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, do you have do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher, and I would like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krasniqi. Please be seated. Mr. Krasniqi, you'll first be examined by -- it will be you, Mr. Kearney? By Mr. Kearney, who's counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you, members of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Could you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I am Jakup Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Could you please tell us your date of birth, sir.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I was born on the 1st of January, 1951.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I was born in Negrovce village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, last week here in The Hague on May 23rd and 24th, did you provide a statement to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: After making that statement, were you given an Albanian copy of that statement to review for accuracy?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I read it and I signed it afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: In addition to reviewing that document, did you also review a series of annexes that were attached to that document?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And were -- did you make comments about those annexes which were included in the statement that you signed?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I made some short comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the Court's permission ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the Court's permission, at this time I'd like to show the witness 65 ter Exhibit 1346, if we may.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, can you see that document, the title page, the first page, in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: May we scroll down to the signature portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, do you recognise your signature on that document?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, it's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you if this statement reflects what you would say in court today if you were asked the same questions that you were asked during that statement last week?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: What I've already stated in my statement, I'm going to state it here too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit Number P328, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection? I hear of no objections, then P328 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have no objection to it, but I do make one comment which is there is no indication in the statement made what questions were asked, so there's an assumption that's being made, however I certainly have no objection to the statement coming in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Please proceed, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, also in that statement at paragraph 9 you say that you told the truth during your testimony in the Limaj trial here in The Hague in 2005. Is that accurate, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: You were also asked if you were asked the same questions that you were during the course of your Limaj testimony in this trial, you would give the same answers. Is that also true?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, it is also true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I would seek to tender that document now if the Court, as it mentioned earlier, wants to take that matter under submission, that's fine. I would notify the Trial Chamber that I did ask the Defence last week if there would be an objection to the admission of that document, and my understanding is that there was not. So I would tender it at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, my position and in this respect I speak only on behalf of Mr. Haradinaj, is that I have no objection to the transcript being admitted; however, as will be obvious, cross-examination in that case was directed to the issues in that case. And whilst we are all grateful to the Prosecution for shortening evidence in chief, I hope Your Honours will bear with me if the usual ratio of evidence in chief to cross-examination is disturbed by that process because there are issues I need to explore in cross-examination which clearly were not explored in cross-examination in Limaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In other words, Mr. Kearney's been kind enough to indicate that he expects to be less than an hour in chief --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course -- the Limaj testimony, of course, is -- stands no need to repeat it but that should not shorten the reasonable time to be granted --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to the Prosecution. That's understood. Then, Mr. Kearney, I have therefore, the transcript for the Limaj case that is transcript pages, I take it that will be uploaded soon, I'm -- have 3285 up to and including 3493. Then about the exhibits dealt with in the testimony in Limaj, same position, no objection, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No. I think Your Honours will have appreciated that the exhibits attached to this witness's 92 ter statement involve a considerable degree of duplication with the exhibits that were exhibited in the Limaj testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I, therefore, suggest, Mr. Kearney, that you go through the attachments to the Limaj testimony and the attachments to the -- that is, the -- that is the 19 documents attached to the statement and see whether there are any doubles in it and then make a final list so that we have -- finally we have then three items: That is, one, transcript; second, witness statement 23rd and 24th of May of this year; and then attachments, either to both or to one of these, and then have perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think unless I'm much mistaken, all of the appendices to the 92 ter statement are -- I see that I am mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you are mistaken. Please proceed. We'll get the final list from Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, as my colleague suggested, I do intend to be very brief in my direct examination today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: -- and to the Trial Chambers --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: -- I intend to focus on four areas.
