The first one is the factual basis for the KLA communiques themselves, with particular emphasis regarding the Dukagjini Zone; secondly, the military operations carried out by the KLA in 1997 and the early part of 1998; thirdly, discipline procedures for KLA soldiers; and lastly, the process involved in ordering the death of a collaborator, with an emphasis again on the Dukagjin Zone. So, Mr. Krasniqi, those are the areas I will ask you about today. And the first question has to do with the actual factual basis for the communiques and the statements that were made that are reflected as annexes to your statement of last week. I want to ask you, sir: Where did the actual operational details come from? When you reported in either a communique or an article or an interview about certain KLA actions having been taken in certain subzones, where did that information come from, please, if you could tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I do apologise for interrupting so soon, but given a close reading of this witness's testimony in the Limaj case, it does, with respect, seem to me that there was an antecedent question which is to what extent did this witness himself author the operational details in the communique of military activity. Because the question makes an assumption which is not, in my judgement, supported by the transcript in Limaj that this witness was personally the author of those parts of the communiques that deal with military activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I would, with all respect to my colleague, very much disagree, Mr. President. The -- it's very clear from the transcript and from his 92 ter statement that this witness was a member of the General Staff at all times when the communiques at issue were made. And he is very much able to talk about the process of how communiques were assembled and where the information that contributed to them came from. And if the Court would like, I can start off with concrete examples to lead the witness through if that would help.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry, just to make it clear, I have no objection at all to this witness giving evidence about methodology --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's just -- I do understand that you understand that you consider the authorship to be slipped in where is there's not and I'm not really certain that Mr. Kearney is -- that is what Mr. Kearney did, as a matter of fact. He was, I think, talking about communiques and reports and he was thinking about what were the sources of information, irrespective of whether this witness himself authored the communiques or not. He could have observed what others may have done. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: It should also not be taken for granted that this gentleman was at all relevant times a member of the General Staff with these responsibilities. So I didn't want that to just slip under the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: -- the mat as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, please proceed in a way you did and you have the -- the signals given to you are not unnoticed, I take it. Please proceed, and let's try to intervene not too early. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I wanted to ask that question again. Do you have it in mind, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: The question was -- and we're talking now generally. We'll talk about specifics of individual communiques in a moment, but just in general. When a communique was issued by the KLA General Staff regarding operational activity in the subzones, where did the General Staff gain that information that went into the communiques, please?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I think that in my statement in the Limaj trial I've already explained this issue; however, I can do it again. At that time I stated that the political process and the political responsibility was separate from the operational one. And the organisation was very much limited. As for the communiques of the KLA General Staff, these communiques were issued by the operational units and they were published on behalf of the General Staff. At the time when the communiques were written or compiled, I was not the person in charge and I did not take part in compiling them or in deciding whether they should be published or not. We dealt mainly with the political statements of the KLA General Staff in which we described the policy of the General Staff and the KLA in general. In other words, the communiques were mostly related to the operative wing of the army. And at that time, this army was more of a guerilla army than a properly organised modern army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Perhaps we can better proceed, Your Honour, by pulling up an example. I'd like to, if I may, call up 65 ter 1346, this is annex number 5 to the 92 ter statement. And I'm going to be referring to page 1 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In order to save time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- I'm sorry. I know that Mr. Kearney has a file of paper copies of the annexes to this witness's statement, and given that there may be a number of documents to be examined, I certainly would have no objection to him providing the witness with the annexes to his 92 ter statement on paper so that whilst things are being loaded examination can continue. Otherwise we may waste some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: That's correct. I brought an Albanian version of the annexes for the witness to save time. I'm happy to, with the Court's permission, to give it to him at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There's no objection against that I see from the Defence. You are allowed to do that. I suggest that once we have -- if you could prepare an index from what you showed to the witness, we then later assign exhibit numbers to them. But we now know that annex 5 is shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I'm informed by our case manager that this is -- the page numbers in the 65 ter exhibit are 24 and 25, if that helps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, can you open your folder there to annex number 5. Do you have that in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Excuse me, I left my glasses in the waiting room and I cannot see the page now very clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then if someone could get the glasses of Mr. Krasniqi. Madam Usher, your assistance is appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, since this is a rather short sentence, perhaps I could read it orally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you read it to the witness, then please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, this is about two-thirds of the way down the document for those reading in English. I'm going to quote a sentence from this document which was published in Pristina Bujku on 5 December 1997. "On 27 November, the police station at Irzniq was attacked. The Serbian policeman Dragan Davidovic was killed and two others were wounded." Now, Mr. Krasniqi, does that fit with your -- even though you can't read that document, does that fit with your memory of what it says, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The actions carried out by members of the Kosovo Liberation Army are described in the communique. And this communique, of course I read it afterwards as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: This is communique number 40, reported in December of 1997. Do you know who composed this communique?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Was it someone on the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: In my statement during the Limaj trial and also a few days ago, I've already explained that the staff was dispersed in several locations. There was a limited number of General Staff members who were in Kosovo acting in illegal way, while another part was operating in Albania and in some European countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Krasniqi, thank you for that answer, but I'm -- my question is much more simple. Do you know who composed this document?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I already told you that I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Was this communique or were communiques such as these, the ones that were numbered, we're going to refer to several of them today, but this number 40 communique, was that sent to Pristina Bujku newspaper by someone from the General Staff or by someone from an operational zone?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The communique could have been sent by a person who at the relevant time was designated to submit these communiques to Bujku or to other newspapers or media.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And who would have been designated to submit those communiques to Bujku?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I don't know at that time who was the person who was designated. I was acting clandestinely at the time, so I could not communicate with the mass media.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, does it help your memory to hear the following sentence from your statement that you gave to the Prosecution last week. This is in the statement regarding annex 5, I'm going to quote: "The report references UCK communique number 40. The contents of the article are an accurate reflection of this communique as issued by the UCK General Staff." Now, Mr. Krasniqi, did you make that statement to the Prosecution last week?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. I said that the content is the content of the General Staff. The General Staff did not object to this communique and it was accepted by the General Staff. This is what I also said in the Limaj trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Now, sir, last week in your statement - I'm going to refer the Trial Chamber and my colleagues to the last clause of this sentence regarding annex 5 - you say: "... This communique as issued by the UCK General Staff." Now, did the UCK General Staff issue this communique or not, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I've already said before and I'm saying it again today, KLA General Staff, and this is what I said in the Limaj trial as well. And I don't think there's any difference between what I've said then and what I'm saying now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Now, sir, in this same communique, this is number 40, this is annex number 5 which I believe you have in front of you now, there are -- there is information, is there not, that comes from different operational zones; namely, zone 1 is represented, the Dukagjini Zone is represented. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: All the information in the communique comes from the KLA, from the Kosovo Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer, but I'm asking you: Was it the role of the General Staff to collect operational data from different subzones, put them into communiques, and pass those communiques on to the media?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The question that you're asking assumes that the General Staff lived and worked in comfortable premises and worked in normal conditions. The General Staff worked clandestinely and it was difficult to do an organised and systematic work that you're putting here. The conditions were very difficult, very limited. This material is propaganda material to raise the morale of the citizens, but of course the KLA was far from being a proper, organised army, especially in the time -- at the time when we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: After you became the spokesperson for the KLA, did you make -- or did you have regular contact with the press?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I became spokesperson of the KLA in June 1998. This was the official time when I started to work as -- in that position. At that time we communicated with the press or, to put it in a better way, the domestic media and international media were interested to get information from us about the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And on those occasions when you contacted the press after you became KLA spokesperson, when you gave the press operational data about what was going on in the field, where did you get your information from?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: During that time we received the information from the subzones of the KLA, mainly by satellite telephones; and on the basis of the information received, we also compiled the political statements and the communiques of the KLA, but always as propaganda material.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And the political statements and the communiques of the KLA, before you became the spokesperson, were they constructed in the same way, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I don't know about the earlier period because I was not author or participant in compiling those communiques.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: When you told us in your statement last week that the information contained in the annexes was accurate, how were you able to make that statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- be clear what Mr. Kearney is putting. The passage he's put so far is that the contents of the article, newspaper article, is an accurate reflection of the communique, whereas what he's now putting is that the information contained in the annexes is accurate. What the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, Mr. Kearney is returning to his original question which we find at the end of page 51, "Does that fit with your memory of what that says," although not very clearly we have -- now -- I think everyone has now moved around two issues. The first one is whether the newspaper reflects what was in the communique, and then another matter, whether what is in the communique and therefore in the newspaper article, whether that reflects what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it you are aware, Mr. Kearney, that these two issues are on our table and that we clearly make a distinction between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I am, and perhaps to assist the Trial Chambers and my colleague, I'll be -- I'll refer to one particular document and ask questions about that. This will be annex number 3, which is 65 ter Exhibit 1346, again at page 17 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry to press, but just to be absolutely clear, the statement that is in this witness's evidence that refers to annex 5 deals with the first of those two propositions, whereas annex 3, I accept, is a statement that deals with the second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have not yet looked at 3, but as far as 5 is concerned that seems to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, do you have annex 3 in front of you, sir, in a language you can understand?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: This was an article published in the Pristina Kosovo Daily Report on 20 October 1997; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: In your statement of last week you say the following words, and please tell us if these are accurate or not: "The actions described in the document did occur at the time and were carried out by the operative wing of the UCK. The report accurately reflects the information given by the UCK to the media." I want to ask you if those two sentences are correct as well?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, they're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Krasniqi, is: How do you know that those actions actually occurred, the ones that are reflected in that document?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I think that this is a superfluous question. I lived in Kosovo. I followed all the political events and other events that occurred in Kosovo, and how could I not know? I also am a close relative of Ardijan Krasniqi, who was killed. I've also written a book that has this information. I wrote a book on this period, so I know all these events as a participant in the political occurrences in the -- in Kosovo in the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, the question was not superfluous, and as a matter of fact you have not answered the question. The question is: Where did you get your knowledge from about these or this event happening? Even politicians hear, see, read, from whatever source. That's what Mr. Kearney would like to know: How do you know that this event took place? And you could not refer to your general knowledge as a politician, but on the specific event Mr. Kearney would like to know where you got the information from.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I do apologise again and I do very much appreciate Your Honour's question, but if it's to be answered then the witness needs to be directed to a specific event. And what happens with a number of these communiques is that they are a melange of different incidents and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, I take it that at this moment the witness has the original of this on his screen before him.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So -- of course I have not seen that. If there are more events there, then the first question would be about all the events I take it, whatever is described as we find in his 65 ter statement. The actions, plural, described in the document did occur at the time, and the question by Mr. Kearney is: How did you know about these events, that is, more than one, took place. Could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All these events that are described in the document I learned about them from the media. The press, radio, television.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Did you, while you were on the General Staff, Mr. Krasniqi, have contact with KLA soldiers in the operational zones themselves?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: What period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Not in 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In 1997, correction of the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in 1998 I almost had daily contacts with the soldiers and with the operational units of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I want to refer you to the beginning part of annex number 3. I'm going to read to you the first two sentences of that document. "A clandestine group calling itself UCK has claimed responsibility for a couple of attacks at the Serbian police stations and a settlement of Slavic refugees. In communique faxed to the media, the UCK said that it had carried out (without specifying the time) attacks at 'Grlica of Ferizaj [Urosevac], Balince of Kline, Baballoq of Decan [Decani], and Qellopek and Kliqine of Peje.'" Now, first of all, am I accurately reading that sentence from annex number 3?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, the sentence is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Now, in your statement of last week you said that this report accurately reflects information given by the UCK to the media. I want to ask you: How did you learn about that -- those events, those attacks on those police stations?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I will repeat what I said earlier. I learned all these from the media, from the newspapers that published these events the next day, from the radio, and also the Albanian television.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Let me ask you a slightly different question. Was it the policy of the KLA to target Serbian police -- to target Serbian police during this period of 1999 and early 1998 up until March of 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry, I think Mr. Kearney misspoke himself. I don't think he meant 1999 and early 1998 but 1997 and early 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: That is what I meant if I didn't say that, thanks to my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It appears on the transcript. Perhaps if you repeat your question, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Was it the policy of the KLA to target Serbian police during 1997 and early 1998 up until March of 1998?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The Kosovo Liberation Army was formed just for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: So I assume, Mr. Krasniqi, that means yes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And if you know, was that the practice in the Dukagjini Zone as well?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It was true for other zones as well, so it was true for the Dukagjini Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Was it also the policy of the KLA to target civilians during this same time-period?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I have explained this question in the Limaj trial, and I will repeat again. The policy of the KLA was not directed against civilians of any ethnicity. It was a policy that was directed against the repressive apparatus of the Serb regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, the reason I ask you that question is in annex number 3, which you still have in front of you, at the end of the first full paragraph it says that: "Attacks at the Serbian police stations and a settlement of Slavic refugees." And then later on, this is in the third paragraph, it refers to an attack of "a settlement of Serb and Montenegrin refugees at Baballoq village of Decan." Do you see that in the statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I see it, but this is not a paragraph from a Serb communique. This is something that was reported by a foreign news agency, and I'm repeating again; this was not the policy of the KLA, to attack civilians. In this bundle of documents you have annex number 2 which says completely an opposite thing to what this statement says here. This is, I repeat, a statement from a news agency, a foreign news agency, and has nothing to do with the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Was there an attack on Slavic refugees in Baballoq -- in Baballoq?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: There might have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: In fact, in your statement last week, referring to this same annex, annex 3, you said that: "The report -- the report accurately reflects information given by the UCK to the media." Isn't that correct, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I was speaking about the parts that are in inverted commas. I never said then and I'm not saying now that the part that is quoted is correct. I'm not speaking here about the accuracy of the foreign agency and their statement. I cannot take that responsibility. And I think my words are being misused here. I'm saying that the quoted parts have been taken as accurate, but the comments that have come from other sources I cannot testify to their accurateness. That was the policy of a certain news agency that made that statement; it was not the policy of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: When you were given a copy of annex 3 in Albanian to read, were those statements included about the refugee camps in Baballoq in your Albanian statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm going to object at this stage if I may, and could the witness remove his earphones before I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not -- may I first ask you, Mr. Krasniqi, do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't understand English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you take off your earphones for a second, Mr. Krasniqi. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's perfectly clear, as is the case with a number of these exhibits which are newspaper reports of communiques, that part of the newspaper report reflects the communique and part of it reflects news reporting. And it's not the communiques themselves that the Prosecution has exhibited but newspaper articles which quote from them. And to take this example, in the second paragraph, there is a quotation from the communique referring to a KLA attack on Baballoq. Now, we've heard other evidence in this case that Baballoq was an area where there was a settlement that at one time was used by refugees and at other times was used by Serb forces. The comments that appear here which seek to identify Baballoq as a refugee settlement as the target of the attack are comments of the newspaper. Now, with respect, this needs to be done with accuracy if we're to establish the sources and knowledge of the sources, and what the witness says in his statement in relation to this, Your Honour, sees it at -- in relation to annex 3 is the actions described did occur and the report accurately reflects the information given by the UCK to the media. Well, the information given by the UCK to the media is that part of the communique which is set out in the newspaper article. And this is going to be a recurrent problem because of the way that this material is being exhibited. This witness is being asked to give evidence about the accuracy of sources that he didn't at the time have privy to, which have been reported in newspapers as part of a composite article. And if Mr. Kearney's going to make the point he needs to make it carefully and accurately; otherwise, it's impossible to know and it wasn't, with respect, made with the accuracy with which it should have been made in the Limaj trial at all. Otherwise it's impossible for the Trial Chamber to disentangle what this witness is really saying about the reliability of the sources of the information on which he's being asked to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in addition, with regard to the specific issue of the settlement at Baballoq, the information is that, "The Serb media reported last week ..." And then it goes on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, my question to this witness was very simple: Was this statement in his Albanian version of the document and that was all. And I think that's a worthy area of inquiry of this witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's not the question I'm objecting to, or the form of it, it's the line of the questioning and the assumptions that underlie it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, it's not the question as such, but Mr. Emmerson has expressed some concerns. I could even add to that that talking about issuing communiques, saying that we just issued communiques on the basis of media sources, whereas at the same time these communiques, as we find in the statement, served to inform the media, which brings a bit of a circular. Therefore, I would endorse Mr. Emmerson's observations that we should clearly distinguish between sources where the communiques reflect what happened or what the sources said at that time. I'm not saying that you're not doing that adequately, but it is a very sensitive issue. If you are aware of that and since there was no objection against the last question, please proceed. And then the witness, of course, in order to hear the question, should put his earphones on again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I'm going to ask my last question again, sir. In this document, this is annex number 3, in your Albanian version of that document, is there mention of the attack on the refugee camp near Baballoq?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: In the annex that you have in front of you, annex number 3, in your Albanian version of that document, is there a mention of the attack on the refugee camp at Baballoq?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I'm just going to very briefly now go through with you some of these annexes. I'm going to ask you if these were documents or statements or communiques issued by the UCK General Staff. I'm going to start with annex number 1. Was that a communication issued by the UCK General Staff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The English page 10, I do understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Same question for annex number 2, sir: Was that communique issued by the UCK General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Again, with respect, both to the previous question and the present one, the question should be in the form: Is that a report of a communique? We are not looking at a communique.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: That's a valid point by Mr. Harvey. Thank you to my colleague, and I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Again referring you to annex number 2, Mr. Krasniqi, is that a report of a communique made by the UCK General Staff to the media, in this case Koha Ditore?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The report speaks of a KLA communique, yes. In other words, this report was made or compiled on the basis of the text of the communique.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And my question goes one step further: Was that communique issued by the KLA General Staff?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I already stated that as long as these communiques bear the stamp of the KLA, of course they came from the General Staff of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Krasniqi, we've already talked about annex 3. I want to move to annex 4 very briefly. This was a report carried by Tirana TVSH television network on 24th November 1997. Was this based -- was this report based on a communique issued by the KLA General Staff?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: We've talked about number 5. Moving to annex number 6, this is an article published in the Pristina newspaper Bujku on 8 January 1998. Is this a report of a communique issued by the UCK General Staff?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Moving now to annex 7. This is another article printed in the newspaper Bujku --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: -- to interrupt yet again. I don't know whether the witness draws a distinction between central staff and General Staff, but it is certainly true that the previous report was of a communique allegedly signed by the Central Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please verify that, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, you just mentioned that regarding annex number 6 that was printed in Bujku, that it was a report reflecting a communique by the UCK General Staff. I want to ask you: Is there a difference in your mind between General Staff and Central Staff?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It is -- both terms refer to the same body or organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I want to move on now to annex number 7. Again, this is an article in the Pristina newspaper Bujku. Is that a report of a communique issued by the UCK General Staff?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you the same question about annex number 8, another newspaper article in Bujku. Is that a report of a communique made by the UCK General Staff?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Same question as to number 9, please. This is yet another article published in Bujku, this one 11 March 1998.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I would give you the same answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Would your answer be the same for annex 10? This is a report published in the Paris Agence France Presse on 11 March 1998, is a report of a communique or a communication made by the KLA General Staff?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, the report is based on a KLA General Staff communique.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Krasniqi, without going through annexes 11 through 19, we certainly can individually, but as you said in your statement last week, aren't they all media reports of communications made by the KLA General Staff?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I have already confirmed this about the communiques, that they were of political nature, in the Limaj trial I've said this. I've said this two or three days ago and I'm repeating myself now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And we understand that. My question is very simply: These were based on communications made by the KLA General Staff, were they not?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I believe that Mr. Kearney is mis -- is in a certain number of regards misstating the very information upon which he's relying in the annexes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the answer's clear. I'm ready to move on to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, there comes a question to my mind at this moment. Mr. Krasniqi, you have at various occasions now said that it was propaganda, it was of a political nature, et cetera. Do you intend to say that whatever may have been in these communiques might well be not true? Is that your message or not? I mean, we are going around what seems to be the real issue. Are you saying that these communiques -- well, they were issued, but political, propaganda, so therefore whether true or not is -- could certainly not accept them to reflect the truth. Is that what you want to say? Then it becomes clear to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would say the following. The events as such are not a propaganda. They occurred and cannot be eradicated, but having in mind the level of organisation of the leadership of the KLA General Staff, they contain more than what was there in reality. The purpose was to make the Albanian people in Kosova think that the KLA is a well-organised army. So whenever we speak of KLA General Staff and other levels of organisation, much more was said in the communiques as means of propaganda. Your Honour, you may well be aware of the fact that propaganda is used in modern times as well by modern armies as well, and when I say "modern armies," I refer to armies that are well-organised and have a long tradition of organisation which operate in much more sophisticated conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So therefore, if I understand you well, if a communique says something about a KLA attack on a police station, then what you would say is that will have taken place, but in interpreting this information don't think that it also means that the KLA was a well-organised armed force, but that we should cautiously interpret this action, this KLA action, which consisted of an attack on a police station. Is that the message you give us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm just anxious that -- there is a follow-on question which is then: What is the basis of the witness's knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. You can put that question to the witness at a later stage. We have already tried to explore that and I do agree with you that that's not in every respect, for the full hundred per cent, clear but parties can explore that. Mr. Kearney, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I want to move on to a different topic for a moment regarding crimes committed by KLA soldiers, if they occurred or not. I want to ask you: Did any of the different zones, the subzones, in 1998 report crimes having been committed by individual KLA soldiers to the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know whether Mr. Kearney means to throw in the entirety of 1998 or whether he wants to break it down at all. This question appears to me to be rather broad, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As the witness did before, sometimes we can wait and see whether the witness makes any further specification as far as time is concerned. Say, to the extent you are asking about the first then -- so therefore we should give an opportunity to Mr. Kearney to generate a flow of evidence, and if it -- matters remain unclear, we'll certainly clarify them but I'd like to have the interventions and the objections reduced. Mr. Kearney, at the same time, the Defence is seeking precision which I would certainly not discourage you to find. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And as a foundational matter I'm going to ask the same question, Mr. Krasniqi, again. In 1998, were any crimes reported to the General Staff from any of the subzones regarding actions committed by KLA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: First of all, I believe that the KLA members did not commit crimes, even if they wanted to, certainly there were no conditions and means for them to carry out crimes. In the second statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I'm going to stop you here. The question was not whether you believed that crimes were committed. The question simply was whether any -- in 1998, were any crimes reported to the General Staff from any of the subzones regarding actions committed by KLA soldiers. So what Mr. Kearney wants to know is whether the General Staff received such reports. True or not is another question, but that's the question, and not whether you believe that crimes were committed, could have been committed. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The General Staff never received information regarding any crime possibly committed during the war period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Did the General Staff have a system in place for disciplining KLA soldiers in 1998 if there had been a crime reported to the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The General Staff did not receive such reports and neither had the proper, appropriate mechanisms to undertake measures for something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Was the disciplining of soldiers the responsibility of subzone commanders during 1998?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The responsibility in the way we were organised was quite difficult to be taken upon by the commander of the zone, because every zone was divided in physical terms because the largest part of Kosova was occupied by the Serbian police and military forces. And in many zones, the units acted separately. So there wasn't a proper organisation and regular communication, so the possibility to discipline in the entire space was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Moving on now to my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say "the entire space," are you referring to zones or are you referring to the whole of the country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The whole Kosova was divided, and the zones, as such, the KLA zones I mean, acted separately. For example, there was a possibility for a battalion or a unit of the KLA to act completely separately from another battalion or unit. This is a well-known fact for that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And subzones, because the question was focusing on subzones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kosova was divided into subzones in the beginning, but as of November 1998 the subzones were named zones. So we might mix up things when we say "subzones" and "zones," but in fact they refer to the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kearney -- by the way, I'm looking at the clock. If you could find a suitable moment somewhere in the next five minutes for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: This actually is a good time, Your Honour. I'm moving into my last topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll have a break, Mr. Krasniqi. We'll resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I want to now move into the final topic that I want to cover with you today, and that's the issue of collaborators. At page -- before the break at page 68, line 15, when you were asked a question by the Court you said the following: "The events as such are not a propaganda. They occurred and cannot be eradicated." And I believe at the time you were talking about attacks on Serbian police officers. I want to ask you the same question about attacks on collaborators. Are the attacks on collaborators that are mentioned throughout the annexes events that actually occurred?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The events occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, was it the policy of the KLA to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, you certainly will not have forgotten what Mr. Emmerson said earlier, what's the source of the knowledge of these events to have occurred. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: In that regard, Your Honour, I will ask permission to recall annex 5 which is 65 ter Exhibit 1346 to 24 -- between pages 24 and 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Can we scroll down just a little bit, Madam Registrar, to the sentence which begins: "On the evening of 28th November," please. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, on -- in annex 5 there is the following quote. I want to read it to you and I'm going to ask you if it's an event that occurred and I'm going to ask you then what you base that knowledge on. "On the evening of 28 November, Dalip Dugolli, a collaborator and one of Milosevic's most trusted men, was killed in the village of Petreshice near Shtime." First of all, did I read that correctly? Is that an accurate quote from that document?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: You read it correctly. I have answered this question several times. I got the information about this case from the media, from television, the radio, and the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Did you talk with any units on the ground, any operational KLA units, about this event?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I communicated with the units on the terrain after I was made spokesperson of the General Staff of the KLA, and I took this position after March 1998. I got my information from the media. I have nothing else to add to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm hesitating. I wonder if the witness might repeat the date on which he took the position, because I'm slightly concerned there may have been a translation error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Well, I could -- our transcript reads that you took the position as spokesperson of the General Staff after March of 1998; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was on the 10th of June, 1998, and it was published in the media on the 12th of June, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would have one other question for you in relation to the document just shown to you, that was annex 5. You said: "I learned this from the media." Do you know how those who prepared the communique learned about the armed attacks described in that communique?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where they got the information from, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At later stages I take it that -- when you had become spokesperson, do you know such a communique of this kind describing operations by units or forces of the KLA, would such information be sent to the General Staff by the forces or units that were involved in this type of activity, that's when you had taken that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After I became spokesperson, the information came to the General Staff from the operational zones, but also from the various units that acted separately from these zones, mainly by satellite telephone that we were using at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So therefore, in your experience, the source of knowledge came, to say it, from the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Generally, the source of information came from the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: In this particular document, Mr. Krasniqi, in the first line it says: "A fax reached our office yesterday containing communique number 40 of the Kosovo Liberation Army and signed by the 'Central Staff of the UCK.'" ? First of all, do you see that in your document?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Are you asking me if I see it in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: No. I'm asking you to look at annex number 5 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In your --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: -- in your packet there. Please look at the first line of that document in the Albanian that you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Oh, there it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And as you look at that, I'd like to read you the sentence again. This is an article published in Pristina Bujku on 5 December 1997. The first sentence reads: "A fax reached our editorial office yesterday containing communique number 40 of the Kosovo Liberation Army and signed by the 'Central Staff of the UCK.' The communique states: 'By a decision of the Central Staff, armed units of the UCK continued their liberation operations during November.'" First of all, is that an accurate translation?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, it's an accurate translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Sir, do you have any reason to doubt that that informing was communicated to Pristina Bujku by the Central Staff of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Of course, at the time somebody designated by the General Staff of the KLA has sent this to Bujku or other press bodies. And because there has been no opposition or contradiction to this, I don't think that the General Staff can deny that this was from the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And you stated earlier in your 92 ter statement that you believed this information to be accurate. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I stand by it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: For instance, in the second full paragraph when it talks about a hand-grenade attack being carried out on 11 November against the house of Tomcic --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Mr. Emmerson, I was about to ask Mr. Kearney about his reference to the 92 ter statement, which says that "The contents of the article are an accurate reflection of this communique as issued by the UCK General Staff." Mr. Kearney, if you refer to the 92 ter statement saying that you believed this information to be accurate, that is not very clear, unless there's any other line you could draw our attention to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I can Your Honour. This is -- and begging the Court's pardon. This -- I was referring --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: -- an answer this witness gave in the Limaj trial. This is 65 ter Exhibit 1349.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, then you were, therefore, referring to a 92 ter transcript rather than a statement, because as I said earlier we have a transcript and a statement. If you could guide us to the relevant --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I will, and first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and has that received an exhibit number already, Madam Registrar? The --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is -- this is just two pages of the transcript. I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: -- It is not our intent to tender these two pages on their own --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I do understand. But if it has a number then I can easily look it up in e-court, that's the only thing, and if I have no number yet, then for the Chamber at least it's more difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I invited Madam Registrar to make sure that it's on the screen so that we know exactly what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down to -- this is page 3322, to line 17, please. And the portion of the text I'm referring to, Your Honour, goes into the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May I make the point. Your Honour anticipated my objection in relation to the 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If, in fact, this is a reference to the 92 ter transcript, it is bedeviled with the same flaw as all of the Limaj references; namely, that once the witness is given an opportunity to comment, there's no explanation or exploration --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's why I wanted to look at it to see if we have a better source there for -- otherwise, Madam Registrar, if the two pages could be printed out for me so that I could have a look at it. And you could continue meanwhile, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Sir, in Exhibit Number 5 there are several specific attacks are described. I just mentioned a hand-grenade attack which was carried out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: You are speaking of annex number 5, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Further down in the document in a sentence beginning with: "On 26 November a special UCK unit attacked Golesh aerodrome. A Cessna 310 aeroplane was hit and brought down and five enemies were killed." I want to ask you sir, first, if you believe that to be accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And by "accurate," you mean that this event took place as described here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The event occurred, but whether it was a real attack I cannot say. This probably was to the service of the propaganda war, and in proving the quality of organisation and attacks of the KLA. I don't think that at the time the KLA had the weapons necessary to bring down an aeroplane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From what altitude was it brought down, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't know. I know that the plane came down, but whether it was as a result of an attack by the KLA, I don't know. I don't think, I don't believe, that the aeroplane could be brought down by the weapons of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, what do you know about it? You say it took place. What do you know about the incident? What did you learn even if you haven't seen it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I did not say, "attack". I said, "the event happened". I do not live far from the place where this aeroplane came down. I think that the aeroplane came down because of some internal defect and not because it was attacked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you seen the aeroplane?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you are positive in saying that -- you're very positive in saying the aeroplane came down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's a fact, that the aeroplane came down because it was in the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were there pictures of the aeroplane in the media?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not see any pictures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then stories about the event in the media?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were announcements in the Albanian media, but also in the Serb media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And now what makes you believe that it was a -- something else than described here that brought the aeroplane down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to bring an aeroplane down you need to have sophisticated weapons, and the KLA did not have at its disposal such weapons at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that it very much depends on from what altitude an aeroplane is brought down? That it could make quite a difference if it's from a thousand metres or from 40 metres or from 20 metres or 80 metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying that this was in the framework of the propaganda that we were carrying out at the time. It helped to boost the morale of the KLA, and I think -- I'm not denying that I would be happy if the KLA were able to bring that plane down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't it true that to qualify something as propaganda rather than as a proper reporting of an event suggests that you know what actually happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know the fact that the aeroplane came down, but whether it was because of an attack of the KLA, I cannot say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think, if I may respectfully say so, we're reaching a point in this witness's evidence where we need to take stock of the methodology in which it is being and is being elicited. And I'd like, if I may, to make some submissions on how it ought to be being elicited, because it's not simply about this particular point but whether this witness is giving evidence about something he thinks was done by the KLA, or something he thinks was not in fact done by the KLA, there is no attempt being made to establish ultimately the basis of his knowledge. Unless we are going to go through every incident in these communiques, which as I understand it, the Prosecution are seeking through this witness to tender as evidence of the truth of the facts that they report, some systematic methodology needs to be adopted, applying the Trial Chamber's own rulings about the approach to hearsay material before any proper evaluation can be made, either about what is in the newspaper reports of the communiques or about what this witness wishes to say about what he did or didn't know about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you take off your earphones for a second. The Chamber is not going to do any stock-taking at this moment. It may be clear for the parties on the basis of objections, on the basis of rulings on objections, on the basis of sometimes the Chamber actively asking questions to the witness that the issue you raise has our full attention to the extent that we would end up in a situation where insufficient material is there to make a proper evaluation of the testimony, of course the Chamber will -- will have to face such a situation if that arises. And it's finally the Prosecution, to the best of its abilities, to present its case.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Will Your Honour hear me for one moment on this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Because the way the Prosecution is seeking to present its case involves resort to a transcript which has been admitted under Rule 92, and Your Honour's just had printed out two pages of the transcript which Mr. Kearney said he relied up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we, perhaps so that I read the lines you had page and line number, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The passage begins on 3322 where he's talking about this annex, this same document, the hand-grenade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us -- could you give me the line --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Yes, it's line 17, it begins --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Line 17, if you would just give me a second to read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And over the page to the first two lines of the following page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. From what I see at this moment, Mr. Kearney, the witness testified in Limaj that the event described there, that is, a hand-grenade attack against the house of a certain person, did occur but that at least from this part of the transcript it is difficult to know how the witness got to know about this event. He just says it occurred as described.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And that was my intent exactly, Your Honours, to present that statement to him that these events actually occurred and then go on to ask him how he knows that. And we are, as the Court heard, this witness is dissembling at some level about whether these events occurred or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- I think the matter as such --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I just take this one stage further. That passage that Your Honour has seen and the fracture in the process of reasoning that this Trial Chamber would adopt occurs between lines 2 and 3 on page 3323, where the matter is simply left as an assertion. That methodology is the methodology that was adopted throughout the evidence in chief in Limaj and was not the subject of cross-examination. Now, if the position is - and we all understand it to be the position here - that it is only those passages that the Prosecution elicits directly from this witness and in respect of which the Prosecution establishes what the factual basis for the witness's knowledge or lack of it is, that will be adduced and relied upon in this case, then I'm very happy for Mr. Kearney to continue as he proposes and to ask what was the basis for the knowledge of that hand-grenade attack and that will then be a confined piece of evidence. But if the Prosecution's position is that the assertions, unchallenged as they were in Limaj, that when a witness says everything in that communique as reported in fact occurred, is to be relied upon in any way in these proceedings, then the question arises whether it is necessary to go through each one of these communiques and establish by reference to each factual assertion whether or not the witness is in the position to give any kind of source material beyond saying it percolated up from the ground which provides no basis for assessing reliability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, he makes a distinction there between certain periods, and for certain periods he says he learned it from the media, this was reported in the media, and then of course the issue of what did the media report and what information was given to the media arises.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Particularly -- I do understand, Mr. Emmerson, your concern that the methodology of the Prosecution in presenting its case is not perfect. That's of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It isn't that; it's that I need to know what case I have to meet, and at the end of the day if it is clear that the only passages on which the Prosecution will seek to rely are those of in respect of whom, they have satisfied the Trial Chamber's own criteria for determining what weight is to be attached to hearsay material, by establishing the sources of the witness's knowledge, then I can sit down because it will only be that which is on this transcript which is being tendered as truth of the contents. If on the other hand, the Prosecution is seeking to rely on material that was generically put in evidence in Limaj with no proper examination of sources as going to the truth of the contents then frankly we need to examine all of it and establish what the basis of the witness's knowledge is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid that the matter is a bit more complex. It's not one or the other, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, what is -- in the reports we can read that. There is some testimony about the sources of knowledge of the witness on whether these events have occurred or not. But it's not abundant to say the least. General statements such as, I learned matters from the press, of course, under the circumstances and in view of the purposes of this might make it rather difficult for the Chamber to rely on whether it's the present testimony or the Limaj testimony. It might even lead to a situation where the Chamber would have to decide that it cannot rely on the -- such general statements as given in the Limaj case, as we have seen an example of until now. Therefore, the Chamber urges you that if you want to -- if you want the Chamber to rely on it to give it the strongest basis you can find. Because otherwise it mainly is a report used in publications on events described in the report and later on in the publications. Then that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can be heard just very briefly in response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I'm -- I should have given you an opportunity, at the same time Mr. Harvey was -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: What this witness has told us recently is that, for instance, this communique was made by the General Staff to the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And to say that he just learned things from the media, well the General Staff, a body that he is a member of, is communicating to the media this information which the media then reproduces. So when this witness says, I learned about these things in the media, by his own statement these -- this is information communicated by the KLA General Staff to the media in the first place. So that's my understanding of his testimony. So to say that the information that he learns in the press is completely without basis, I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: -- with all due respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't say that as a matter of fact. I didn't say -- I urged you to give it the strongest basis possible. Which is not exactly the same as what you just said. The Chamber is not going to -- first of all, I'd like to give you an opportunity to finish because I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I'm happy -- I'm not happy, but I'm completely willing to go through 19 documents with this witness and go through fact by fact because I think it's very clear -- at least it is to the Prosecution, that there is reluctance on behalf of this witness to attest to some of the things that perhaps he has in the past. I am very happy or very willing to go through point by point in 19 documents to retrieve a basis from this witness as to every fact averred in all of the documents. I'm trying to pick out -- I realise that the Trial Chamber would probably not grant me the time to do that. I'm trying efficiently to pick out examples, namely, this one, annex number 5, where he said in no uncertain terms in the Limaj testimony that the -- everything that is said here really happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I'm trying to use that as an example to the Trial Chambers to show that this witness believes the events there to be accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it -- it's -- that's not the issue, whether the witness believes or not, but in order to properly evaluate what the basis for this belief is. I mean, I do agree with you -- I do understand what you are doing in relation to Limaj. There the witness said, Yes, it happened. Now, what should the Chamber rely upon in view of evaluating where what the witness says, which often comes down to, I believe it happened, what that belief is based upon. I mean, for the aeroplane now we have even some strong beliefs in different directions that it would be propaganda. At the same time, you may have understood from my line of questioning that to know what is propaganda you have to know where the exaggeration is. And if you have to know where the exaggeration is you have to know what really happened. So therefore, that raises a few issues as well, but of course, the Limaj case doesn't add much to what the witness testified here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from that at that time he also believed it happened. At that time not examined on how he knew and I can imagine that you say , let's take a few examples and see what happens. And you did it on some of these -- well, it's then of course the next question is whether the Chamber is willing at any time to draw inferences on the basis of examples, that's -- Mr. Emmerson is already nodding no, so therefore he tends to disagree with such a possibility. But there of course is -- that is the issue. We see a document which, as the witness says, he has -- that's at least how I understand it, he has no reason to believe that the event described there did not take place. That's how I -- at least how I understand if you say it takes place, but if he hasn't been there himself. The more information the Chamber has to rely upon to accept or not accept the statement that it took place, of course the better the Chamber is placed to evaluate this evidence. Of course, it's a matter of balance. I'm aware of that. Every single detail or general knowledge. Mr. Harvey, you were on your feet as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I've been getting a lot of exercise over here, Your Honour. I'm troubled and it may be a cultural problem, although I don't know that it is since Mr. Kearney and I have at least practiced on the opposite side of the Atlantic as well. My understanding of the duty of a Prosecutor before he calls his own witness a liar, is to explore at least the basis for the -- for so doing. At page 83, line 10, Mr. Kearney said: "And we are, as the Court heard, this witness is dissembling at some level about whether these events occurred or not." Your Honour, in plain English, the word "dissembling" means lying and it seems to me to be at least a very hasty judgement to be making, and I rise not merely to underscore the points that Your Honour has been making yourself but out of fairness to the witness, out of fairness to these proceedings which are being watched and are being listened to, that this is a witness who is sitting here being traduced by the counsel who is calling him and not -- and I hope he will be given by that same counsel an opportunity to deal with the allegations that are being made, in my submission, most unfairly against him at this stage in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether unfairly or not, whether the words were chosen with great care at that moment is another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber, Mr. Kearney, takes it that you have carefully listened to what I said and to what some Defence counsel said and invites you to continue now your examination-in-chief. But taking advantage of what has been said. The Chamber is not going to tell you that you have to explore 19 documents, all the events, or not to do it, or to try to get more general basis for the sources of knowledge. The Chamber leaves that to you. Sufficient observations were made on what the Chamber, the Defence, and perhaps the public will expect from the Prosecution. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May we, though, cease the examination of this witness seven minutes to 7.00 so that I can seek guidance from Your Honour as to how I should prepare my cross-examination with those rulings in mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll reserve a couple of minutes before we adjourn. Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. -- Put your headphones on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you put your headphones on. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, when this communique was made, this is annex number 5, when this was made by the General Staff to Pristina Bujku, you were, in fact, a member of the General Staff. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I was, and I've already explained this at our last meeting, as well as in the testimony in the Limaj trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Can you explain to us, please, what input the General Staff had in forming these communiques to the media.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I will explain it yet again. We are talking about end of 1997. It is true that the actions of the KLA intensified, but the headquarters acted rarely and it was dispersed not in one place due to the clandestine conditions. And we cannot say that this communication was consolidated. Maybe in most of the cases the name of the staff was used, not that the staff members communicated between each other. As I've already said, the General Staff was divided into three parts. One part operated in very difficult conditions and with limited number of staff in Albania --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In Kosovo, correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- another part in Albania, and another part in western European countries, as in Switzerland, for example. Kosova was encircled by the police and army of the Serbian authorities. It was impossible under such conditions for it to exist in that capacity. I wished that the KLA General Staff was of that type, that would be the proper leadership body; but for that period of time, this was quite impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: But this reporting of events that were taking place on the ground in Kosovo, what segment of the General Staff was doing that reporting?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I've already stated that this was done by the operative units and by the persons in charge of the operational part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: For instance, this communique that we're looking at here, this is annex 5, communique number 40, was this a communication with the media made by an operational units?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: As to who and how sent out the communique, I will again tell you that I don't know, but as such the General Staff recognised this communique as its own. So we took it as a communique of the General Staff of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, perhaps that's not what I'm understanding. When you say that the General Staff recognised this communique as its own, can you explain that. Was it a -- did it adopt communications made by individual units on the ground or something else?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: You will receive the same answer from me. I've already explained this. Depending on which unit a certain operation was carried out, that unit designated a person who would inform the General Staff and then the text of the communique was compiled on the basis of the information received.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: This communication from the individual units to the General Staff, how was that made? Was it made by phone? Was it made by courier? How was that made?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the question has been asked, Mr. Kearney, isn't -- or am I wrong, and answered --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we'll ask the witness to try to find out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already answered this question, but I will answer it again. During this time, our main means of communication was telephone. I've already told you, Mr. Prosecutor, that the communication between the members of the KLA in Kosovo and with representatives of KLA living outside of Kosovo was done through telephone. This is what I told you during our meeting last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But this creates new confusion, Mr. Krasniqi. I understood that this type of communiques as we have in front of us was prepared by the KLA General Staff in Kosovo. So when we are talking about communications between those on the ground providing, if they did, information on the basis of which such a communique was given, then we are not talking about -- primarily about communication between those on the ground and General Staff outside Kosovo, but rather, General Staff inside Kosovo. Would the communication with the General Staff who prepared such communiques be similar, that is, by telephone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, by telephone. I will explain it once again. We are speaking of a time when my knowledge as to the way these communiques were written are not clear. I've explained you about the period when I was in charge of communication with the public opinion, that I can be very accurate in what I say. So from that perspective as how we communicated in the later period, I can comment on how it was done earlier. So such a communique could be written by a representative outside Kosovo, but on the basis of information collected from representatives inside Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you have answered a few times a question by saying this or that event which we find in a communique did happen. You cannot eradicate that. That's, I think, the words you used. Now, taking this example, annex 5, I do understand that you were then already a member of the KLA General Staff.
