Apart from who drafted the communique, did you learn as a member of the General Staff, even when not involved in drafting communiques, about the events we now see were described in such communiques? I mean, would you as a member of the General Staff, even if you would have nothing to do with drafting any communique, would you learn about what happened on the 11th of November or the 25th of November what your units would have done at those dates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Kosova is a small area. I was a political worker in Kosova. Of course I learned about these events through other people who had heard about those events. I heard about these events also through media, but also when we would meet with other staff members, members of the General Staff I mean, we also discussed how successful or unsuccessful these actions were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In discussing that, did they, as far as you know - if you don't know, please tell us - rely on information they received from the ground, from the units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the majority of cases, we learned about those events from the information received from the ground. And in my case, as I said earlier, in most of the cases I heard about those events more quickly from the media than from the communication with other members of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kearney, Mr. Emmerson asked for seven minutes. I'm aware that there were frequent interventions by the Chamber. Mr. Emmerson, may I take it that you would like to make your submissions in the absence of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I certainly don't need the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You certainly don't need the witness. Then, Mr. Krasniqi, we have a procedural matter to be discussed for a couple of minutes. We'll resume tomorrow in this same courtroom at a quarter past 2.00. We'd like, therefore, to see you back tomorrow, and I instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given until now and the testimony which still is to be given in the day or the days to come. Madam Usher, could you -- yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the Court releases this witness, could the Court inquire if he actually brought with him copies of the original communiques to The Hague or a book containing them, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I could ask him. Do you -- did you bring -- you have heard the question put by Mr. Kearney. Did you bring any of the original communiques to The Hague or a book which contains such communiques?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't bring it with me, but I gave the members of the OTP two books that I've written and a book with the communiques issued by the KLA so that they would use the original communiques and not foreign media or other organisation documents and reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, of course in view of the answer, the question surprises --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: None of this has been disclosed. We had one disclosure yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's first -- I mean, if Mr. Kearney asks something of which the witness says I brought it already, then there is -- there may well be malcommunication, question could have been misunderstood, or Mr. Kearney might have wanted to ask something different. Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Could we just inquire of the witness who he actually gave these books to. I don't have them, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we could ask the witness. Mr. Krasniqi, to whom did you give the books you were just talking about and when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor knows that these books were submitted to one of his representatives in Pristina on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that -- I take it, Mr. Kearney, that needs some further inquiries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I'll inquire this evening, Your Honour, and have an answer for the Court tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Madam Usher, could you escort the witness out of the courtroom. And the instruction stays as I said before, not to speak with anyone about the testimony. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, whether dealing with media reports or with original communiques, the problem remains the same. The communiques might eliminate the confusion surrounding additional comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But the ultimate problem remains the same, which is that the Prosecution are seeking to tender the content of these communiques as evidence of the truth of their contents. They contain -- essentially the evidence that's that has been given to Your Honours is multiple hearsay; in other words, it's a witness saying, I've seen those communiques, I did not draft them, I didn't even draft the ones that were issued after I was appointed on the 11th of June because I was responsible for political statements and the communiques contained military information which was provided by the operational wing. He was never asked in Limaj for the basis of the knowledge when he made these sweeping assertions about the correctness of the contents, but when asked before Your Honours repeatedly, we get a mixture of a response that it is information that he learned from the media and a response that it is information that percolated up from the grass roots, neither of which provides any basis for assessing the reliability of the material as evidence of the truth of its contents, which is a particularly difficult problem when the witness asserts repeatedly, as he does, that the purpose of the communiques, primarily, was propaganda; in other words, to distort. And sorting out within a situation such as that what is truth and reliable -- reliably sourced material from what is not is an extremely difficult exercise. Now, when I raised the matter earlier on - and this is -- the reason I'm raising it now is it goes to cross-examination tomorrow. When I raised the matter earlier on, I indicated that, provided it is clear, that the only documents, the only statements, upon which the Prosecution seeks to rely as being evidence of the truth of their contents are statements about particular actions in respect of which the basis of the witness's knowledge has been properly laid and explored before the Tribunal, then I have no problem. But if, as, with respect, seems clearly to be the case, the Prosecution here is proceeding as did the Prosecution in Limaj on the fallacious assumption that by getting this witness to say if it's written in the communique it must be true, that this Trial Chamber will be able to evaluate and rely upon the contents, then that leaves me in an impossible position. It's not simply -- I'm trying to be practical about this rather than doctrinaire. I appreciate some of these objections may sound as though I'm nitpicking, but if Your Honour imagines the position that I find myself in. Your Honour indicated on the transcript at page 88, line 17, that for Mr. Kearney essentially to select either between particular passages or between all of those on which he wished to rely was a matter of balance, but Your Honour, for the Defence it's not a matter of balance, it's a matter of fairness. We are entitled to know which of these factual assertions we need properly to challenge and the basis for them. Now, it is for the Prosecution to identify those facts it relies upon and to establish the basis for them. And I can't very well go into cross-examination on the general assumption that if the Prosecution hasn't laid a foundation I don't need to deal with it unless it is clear that that is the basis upon which we are proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, if you would like to respond you have got two minutes to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this approach places the Defence in anything but an impossible position. All the Defence has to do on cross-examination is inquire of the witness how he knows certain things. We just heard from this witness that - and this is something I want to pursue with him tomorrow more - that forces on the ground and units who conducted the operations contacted the General Staff and conveyed information to the General Staff about the operations themselves. And these -- this data is part of what went into the communiques. I believe there is sufficient reliability there for the Trial Chamber to place weight on those events occurring, as this witness himself told us, he believes that the events themselves as described actually occurred and there was a propaganda component as well. However, to simply throw out all these communiques as the Defence seems to be suggesting without further inquiry I think is improper at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I've briefly consulted with my colleagues. I think the -- the issue is clear enough. The less we know about the source of knowledge or belief or -- of the witness in relation to what we find in these documents, of course the more corroboration of another type you would need to give - I'm not saying any weight at all, but to give more than relatively small weight to this material. The Chamber cannot anticipate on what corroboration there still will be. So therefore, although I do understand the concerns that come up in the mind of Defence counsel, they nevertheless have to cope with that situation and have to cross-examine the witness on the basis of the evidence that the witness until now gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I entirely understand. Corroboration, of course, is an entirely separate question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And whether from here or from another, and therefore the Chamber cannot anticipate and say this is how we will use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber at the end of the case will look at the totality of the evidence and we'll also look at the totality of the evidence the Defence will take. Therefore, I at -- I -- my reputation is bad already going over 7.00. Anything that can wait until tomorrow should wait until tomorrow. We will resume quarter past 2.00, Courtroom I, tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 30th day of May, 2007, at 2.15 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.06 p.m.,
